entries.section: 1. The questioning of the prophet Habakkuk:

paragraphs.text: 1 The burden which Habakkuk the prophet did see. 2 O LORD, how long shall I call, and thou wilt not hear? I cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save! 3 Why dost thou shew me iniquity, and lookest upon wrong? for spoiling and violence are before me: and strife ariseth, and contention lifteth up itself. 4 Therefore the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgment proceedeth.

With boldness the prophet cries out to God, saying that he calls upon Him and He does not hear; he cries to Him again and again because of the injustice that prevails among the people, and He does not save the oppressed. So the people of God have turned into a hotbed of injustice, wrong, plunder and strife; there is no one who wants to listen to the Law, nor anyone who accepts a just judgment, but the wicked surround the righteous man to stifle his breath and bring forth judgment according to their own desire.
"How long, O LORD, shall I call, and thou wilt not hear?!
I cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save?!
Why dost thou shew me iniquity, and lookest upon wrong? for spoiling and violence are before me: and strife ariseth, and contention lifteth up itself?!

entries.section: 1. The questioning of the prophet Habakkuk:

paragraphs.text: Therefore the law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgment proceedeth" [2-4].

In a friendly reproach he says: "How long, O LORD, shall I call, and thou wilt not hear?!" For the prophet did not cease to call upon the Lord and cry out to Him, if not with the tongue then with the heart and tears, because of the bitterness of what the people had reached through the injustice of the wicked. He knocks at the doors of God's mercies with his tongue, his heart and his tears, mingling his tears with the tears of the oppressed and his sighs with theirs!

In every generation the children of God stand amazed at the success that the wicked oppressors seem to have, and they say with the prophet David, "I have seen the wicked in great power, and spreading himself like a green bay tree. Yet he passed away, and, lo, he was not: yea, I sought him, but he could not be found" (Ps 37:35-36). The bitterness of Jeremiah's soul, because of the corruption and injustice he saw in his people, reached the point that he said: "Oh that I had in the wilderness a lodging place of wayfaring men; that I might leave my people, and go from them!" (Jer 9:2), and yet Jeremiah, in his love for his people, did not leave them, in spite of the distress he suffered on every level.

entries.section: 1. The questioning of the prophet Habakkuk:

paragraphs.text: We return to the words of the prophet Habakkuk to find in them a revelation of his person: he is a man of God who cannot bear injustice, and so he speaks with his God in an open dialogue without formality, officialdom, flattery or pretense, but speaks out of the unceasing groans of his heart and his tears that do not dry. This is the picture of the man of God, whether priest or of the people, whose prayers do not cease night and day, with the lips as with the heart and the deed... He cries out that God may remove corruption and injustice from fallen humanity, and so raise up every soul holy to Him. Therefore he asks and seeks and cries without ceasing and without despair, confident that God is able to act! The prophet also knew the secret of their evil, that it lies in the deviation from the divine commandment or the Law, for he says, "The law is slacked, and judgment doth never go forth: for the wicked doth compass about the righteous; therefore wrong judgment proceedeth" [4]. The Law, which sets the heart on fire and gives it life, becomes rigid and ineffective if the wicked surround the righteous man and corrupt his mind concerning the commandment.

If the men of God in every age cried out to the Lord because of what they saw of the wicked oppressors, who trifle with the earth, while the righteous live in distress and bitterness, yet because they laid their thoughts and hearts open before the Lord, they increased in honor in the eyes of God. But whoever looks at this state and yields to thoughts of doubt concerning God's care and His governance of the world, his soul is struck with sickness. As St. Augustine says: [Holy Scripture presents the thirty-seventh Psalm as a fitting remedy for the one whose soul is afflicted with this sickness. In brief, this Psalm affirms that the wicked live like grass on the margin of the surface; they appear successful in the winter of this world, but summer is coming and they dry up and burn, for they have no roots in the depths of the soil.]

entries.section: 2. Chastisement by the Chaldeans:

paragraphs.text: 5 "Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for I will work a work in your days which ye will not believe, though it be told you. 6 For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and impetuous nation, which shall march through the breadth of the earth, to possess the dwellingplaces that are not theirs. 7 They are terrible and dreadful: their judgment and their dignity shall proceed of themselves. 8 Their horses also are swifter than the leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves: and their horsemen shall spread themselves, and their horsemen shall come from far; they shall fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat. 9 They shall come all for violence: the look of their faces is forward, and they shall gather the captivity as the sand. 10 And they shall scoff at the kings, and the princes shall be a scorn unto them: they shall deride every strong hold; for they shall heap dust, and take it. 11 Then shall their spirit transgress, and they shall pass over, and offend. This their might is their god."

The Lord's answer to the prophet's question came thus: "Behold ye among the heathen, and regard, and wonder marvellously: for I will work a work in your days which ye will not believe, though it be told you. For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans..." [5-6].

Truly, God keeps silent for a time, not ignoring what happens nor out of lack of concern on His part, but to give an opportunity for return without chastisement from Him; if man does not return from his evil, the Lord Himself undertakes the chastisement, using every means for edification.

A. God is working a work in their days which they would not believe if it were told them... He is long-suffering, but when He chastises He gives a profitable lesson, even if it is severe. As it is written in the Book of Deuteronomy: "Even all nations shall say, Wherefore hath the LORD done thus unto this land? what meaneth the heat of this great anger? Then men shall say, Because they have forsaken the covenant of the LORD God of their fathers" (Deut 29:24-25). And as St. John Chrysostom says: [God did not intend to punish so much as to reform them in the future... God is good and loving, not only when He grants gifts but also when He chastises us, for even His chastisements and punishments are of His goodness, and a great manifestation of His help to us]. He also says that if God drove Adam out of Paradise, it was in order that by his expulsion He might bring him back to Himself... So also, if God allowed the people to go into captivity, it was in order to awaken in them the longing for inner freedom and the yearning to return, not only to the earthly Jerusalem, but also to the heavenly one.

B. He says: "Behold, I raise up the Chaldeans," for He is the Lord of history and its director, who uses even the wicked to accomplish His good divine plan for humanity. The Chaldeans, in their love of plunder, took the people captive, but by divine permission for the repentance of the people, as though God raised up the Chaldeans specially for this work.

C. The Chaldeans point to the enemy of good, to whom we ourselves hand ourselves over as slaves because of our sins; the Lord protects us from him again and again so that we may not fall under his humiliation, but when we insist on submitting to him, the Lord leaves us under his hands for our chastisement. In this spirit St. Paul the Apostle asks the Corinthians to leave the young man who fell with his father's wife, delivered to Satan, to be delivered to chastisement, saying: "In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, to deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus" (1 Cor 5:4).
The traits of the nation of the Chaldeans here correspond to the traits of the enemy of good and his work against us:

entries.section: First: "a bitter nation" [6]

paragraphs.text: The enemy of good is not an individual being but a nation, that is, a kingdom led by the devil as a king who has rulers, authorities and powers (Eph 6:12), who has his angels and his soldiers (Mt 25:41); and it is a bitter kingdom that offers out of its own what it has, namely bitterness, delighting and rejoicing in the misfortunes of others and their destruction; its goal is demolition, not edification.

entries.section: Second: impetuous:

paragraphs.text: The Chaldeans were an object of bitterness to all the nations around them; they knew neither gentleness nor covenants of peace, but only attack and fighting. In this they were an impetuous nation that swoops down on others to take them captive and humble them. So also the devil with all his angels storm the doors of man to enslave and humble him, to work on their behalf. They lie in wait for him, to storm in swiftly at the moments when the doors of the senses or the emotions open, and rush inside to proclaim their kingdom in them. Therefore the psalmist cries: "Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips," lest the enemy storm into his life.

entries.section: Third: marching through the breadth of the earth:

paragraphs.text: The nation of the Chaldeans roamed in every place to seize peoples and kingdoms without hindrance, roaming as though over the whole earth to devour all, but it was not able to rise upward to humble those who had been lifted up from the earth. So the enemy of good sees that the whole earth has opened before him, and he walks in its breadth, so that he is called the prince of this world or its elements.

The limits of the enemy of good are "the breadth of the earth," for he is, as St. Jerome says: [like the serpent that crawls on the earth with its head and tail and the rest of its body, entirely clinging to the earth]. He devours dust, so whoever among us is earthly or of the dust becomes food for him, but whoever lifts his heart up to heaven to practice the heavenly life, without the love of earthly things pulling him down, the enemy cannot snare him!

entries.section: Fourth: to possess dwelling places that are not theirs:

paragraphs.text: The Chaldeans encroached on the property of others and on their persons, reckoning that everything was theirs alone, that it was their right to plunder and possess without hindrance, so long as they had the power and authority. So the enemy of good plunders humanity, which is not the work of his hands nor his possession, but the possession of Him of whom "all things were made by him; and without him was not any thing made that was made" (Jn 1:3). It is the nature of the enemy of good to plunder what belongs to God, in order to set up his dwelling and kingdom in the heart that He made to be His holy temple.

The prophet Jeremiah expressed this satanic trait in the proverb: "As the partridge sitteth on eggs, and hatcheth them not; so he that getteth riches, and not by right, shall leave them in the midst of his days, and at his end shall be a fool" (Jer 17:11). And Origen interprets this proverb, saying: [The partridge, known as a cunning bird, circles around the feet of the hunter so that he is occupied with her until she is assured that her young have escaped, and then she flies away, and the hunter takes neither the young nor their mother; in this she resembles Satan, who occupies man's mind with earthly things so that he obtains neither earthly nor heavenly things. This partridge often sits on eggs that are not hers, and when the eggs hatch the young stay with her until the original mother comes and gives a call that the young understand, and they leave the deceiving partridge and return to their mother. It is a living picture of what happened, for the devil embraced humanity as his young and seduced it with his deceptions, but in the midst of his days the Lord Christ came giving the voice of His love, declaring it practically on the Cross, drawing the deceived humanity to return to its true Creator, and the devil lost what he had acquired without right, and at the end of the ages he will be a fool, for he will perish utterly in the fires of Gehenna.]

Since the devil, like the Chaldeans, possessed dwelling places that were not his, or like the partridge that sat on what she did not hatch, he loses everything, even himself, through the Cross, which returned the believers to their Creator and Savior, and which condemned the devil and all his hosts, since He "took it out of the way, nailing it to the cross; and having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it" (Col 2:15).

entries.section: Fifth: terrible and dreadful:

paragraphs.text: The enemy of good is frightening and fearsome to the man stripped of defense, but the one hidden in Christ Jesus, who "went forth conquering, and to conquer" (Rev 6:2), the enemy cannot terrify him; rather he himself trembles before him. Let us hide in Him who alone is able to "enter into a strong man's house, and spoil his goods" (Mt 12:19). If the enemy is strong, the Lord has bound him with the Cross and drawn away from him his spoils, which are humanity, and the Lord Himself has become the commander of the spiritual battle. Fr. Theophan the Recluse says: [Know that our enemies and all their schemes are in the grip of our Lord Jesus Christ, our divine commander, for whose glory and greatness you fight. And since He leads you in the battle Himself, He certainly does not allow violence to be used against you, nor does He will you to be defeated by the enemy, unless you incline to their side by your own will].

entries.section: Sixth: their judgment and their dignity proceed of themselves:

paragraphs.text: The nation of the Chaldeans is despotic in its opinion, subject to no law but its own whim, and the enemy of good in his dealing with us is governed by nothing but his whim, so discussion with him is of no use. Therefore the Fathers of the Church advise us not to give ear to his words nor to enter into dialogue with him, for his dialogue is full of deceit and is not constructive.

entries.section: Seventh: their horses are swifter than the leopards:

paragraphs.text: In this chapter the divine inspiration gives us a living, realistic picture of the hideousness of the true enemy, the devil, who spends all his energies to enslave us:

In the speed of his movement in preying he is swifter than leopards, and in his cunning, working in darkness, he is fiercer than evening wolves; his sphere of work is without limits, spread in every place setting his nets; his capabilities are formidable; he is able to come from afar to pounce on his prey from where we do not expect; his ability to plunder and flee is like the eagle that snatches its prey and flies off with it; his constitution is the law of injustice, without mercy or understanding; in his nature he is a predatory beast whose face is forward like the beasts; his captives are like the sand, without number; he humbles the king and mocks the princes; his slain are mighty; he shatters strongholds and heaps them up as dust that he uses for the sake of his kingdom; he is wicked by nature.

And now we speak of these traits in some detail. As to the speed of his movement in preying, as we said, he is swifter than leopards. He is swift in movement, full of craftiness and cunning, seizing every opportunity to hunt the soul, watching for the least negligence or slackness to draw the soul into his net. The believers, for their part, are watchful, seizing every opportunity to grow and to enjoy the crown... The spiritual life in truth is seizing opportunities: the enemy seizes the opportunity, and the believer seizes the opportunity. It is a continual spiritual struggle for each to reach his goal. We can sense this from the words of St. Ignatius of Antioch, who hastened to write to the Romans to stop the plan they had made to rescue him from martyrdom, since he counted that as love, but untimely... He counted his martyrdom an opportunity that might not be repeated, so why should they deprive him of it?! He says: [I beg you not to show me kindness out of season, but allow me to be food for the wild beasts, through whom it is granted me to attain to God. I am the bread of God; let me be ground by the teeth of the wild beasts, that they may become my tomb, and leave nothing of my body, so that when I die I may be a burden to no one... Entreat Christ for me that by these means I may be found a sacrifice to God... May I have joy of the wild beasts that are prepared for me, and I pray that they may be found eager to rush upon me, and I will entice them to devour me quickly].

entries.section: Eighth: fiercer than the evening wolves:

paragraphs.text: If the devil moves by day like a leopard with great lightness together with cunning, in the evening he does not stop but goes out like evening wolves to seize. He knows no rest by day nor by night, so it behooves us to persevere without ceasing... even in the moments of sleep our souls say, "I sleep, but my heart waketh" (Song 5:2).

Fr. Theophan the Recluse sees that the believer not only perseveres, guarded against the blows of Satan, but by the power of the Spirit stirs up war against him to seize from him every position he had previously occupied inside the heart, saying: [If you wish, my brother, to gain a swift and easy victory over your enemies, you must wage war without ceasing and courageously against all your passions... Therefore our spiritual warfare must be continual without ceasing, supported by watchfulness and courage of soul, and these can be reached easily if you ask for them as a gift from God. So continue in the battle without hesitation].

Like the evening wolves he works in darkness to hide his tricks and schemes (Eph 6:11). As St. John Chrysostom says: [This enemy fights us not in an open and clear way but by schemes... He does not propose sins to us in their true colors... but presents them in another garment, to make his speech acceptable and disguised].

entries.section: Ninth: their horsemen spread themselves, they come from far:

paragraphs.text: The enemy of good sets his snares in every place, spending all his energies to hunt souls even if the person is in a holy place. He dared to fight the Lord Christ on the pinnacle of the temple, and the Lord permitted him this in order to warn us, assuring us that the enemy fights in every place, at home as at work, in the church as in the street, in the closet where private prayer is made and during communal worship. Wherever he finds us he creeps toward us, in the hope of finding a place in our hearts.

As for his coming from afar, it means that he fights us from where we do not expect. Therefore it behooves us to have a burning spiritual insight that understands the mysteries of spiritual warfare and knows the tricks and deceptions of the devil.

entries.section: Tenth: their horsemen fly as the eagle that hasteth to eat:

paragraphs.text: Origen says: [The eagle can see its prey from a great height, and with snatching speed it swoops on it and flies off, and no one can pull it from its claws. So the horsemen of the devil, or his demons, watch the soul to know when to swoop on it with extreme speed, and through the astounding surprise man descends into sin in a short time to find that he has lost much. If building needs a long time, demolition takes place in simple moments, and if the holy virtues require long striving in the Lord, their demolition is accomplished in simple moments of negligence]. And as St. John Chrysostom says: [A swift blow of the sword, lasting only moments, wounds a man so that he is treated for it perhaps for years, and it may end his life. So the enemy strikes with his sword in our moments of negligence... but these moments spoil the striving of long years!].

entries.section: Eleventh: they come all for violence [9]:

paragraphs.text: The law of the devil, or the constitution by which he works, is the "law of injustice"; he seeks only to deprive us of the greatest good, and to draw us away from the heavenly life, that we may not be bound to the divine law or the truth. St. John Chrysostom says of the demons: [They do not wrestle to gain anything, but to corrupt us... Satan spends all his energy to drive us out of heaven].

entries.section: Twelfth: the look of their faces is forward:

paragraphs.text: Perhaps by this he means that they are not like human beings, who have the lifted face that seeks heaven, but have the trait of predatory beasts that stretch out their faces to prey without tenderness or pity!

entries.section: Thirteenth: they gather captives as the sand:

paragraphs.text: The devil hunts souls without number and takes them captive like sand, for he has been titled "the prince of this world" and "the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience" (Eph 2:2). St. John Chrysostom says: [Why does (the Apostle) call Satan the prince of the world? Because nearly all humanity has gathered around him, and they have become slaves to him by their own will and free choice].

entries.section: Fourteenth: they scoff at the kings, and the princes are a scorn unto them [10]:

paragraphs.text: Every time the people fell into captivity, the king was humbled and the great ones became an object of mockery and ridicule before the victors; when Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem and the cities of Judah captive, he ordered the sons of King Zedekiah slain before his eyes, and put out the king's eyes and carried him to Babylon to mock him. So when a believer falls under the hands of the enemy of good because of his carelessness or slackness, he mocks him.
If we in Christ Jesus, the King of kings, have become spiritual kings (Rev 1:6; 5:10), the devil spends all his energies to take us captive, despising us.

In our study of the Book of Hosea we saw that the king points to the human will, which reigns over man to manage all his affairs, and the princes point to man's energies and gifts... For when the enemy takes a person captive, he mocks his human will, depriving him of it so that he lives the rest of his life as a humble slave doing the will of his new master (Satan), and he squanders his gifts and energies (the princes) to make of them a mockery and ridicule! The enemy of good makes man lose everything: his will, his gifts, his energies, even his body also, and finally carries him with him to where there is perpetual perdition.

entries.section: Fifteenth: they deride every stronghold:

paragraphs.text: Strongholds could not stand before the nation of the Chaldeans, and so also no one can fortify himself, neither by his long experience, nor by his abilities and gifts, nor by rationalistic intellectual knowledge, nor by his dignity or the kind of his work... When the devil laughs at these strongholds, one stronghold remains which, if we cling to it, he cannot approach, namely the Lord Christ, the Rock of ages.
St. Jerome says: [The Lord Christ is the smooth Rock (1 Cor 10:4) on which the serpent cannot crawl, so whoever fortifies himself in Him is protected from the enemy, the old serpent].

entries.section: Sixteenth: they heap dust, and take it:

paragraphs.text: In further humiliation the enemy demolishes the lofty stronghold and turns it into dust, then the enemy returns and uses the dust for the sake of his kingdom, that is, for his benefit. I say this is a bitter picture of the devil's work in the lives of those taken captive by him: he turns their lives into dust, drawing their hearts to the earth and corrupting their nature... and then he uses this dust as earthen vessels bearing his traits to hunt others.

Although the enemy fell from heaven, he does not cease to spend all his energies, not only to deprive his victim of the heavenly life and bring him down to the love of earthly things, but he also uses him to bring others down and deprive them of the heavens that are within them.

entries.section: Seventeenth: their spirit transgresses and passes over; this their might is their god [11]:

paragraphs.text: Their spirit transgresses or changes to what is worse or more wicked, passing from evil to evil, and from iniquity to iniquity... looking to their iniquity and plunder as the might of their god who gives them victory over the peoples. They reckoned that their gods were stronger than the God of Israel, so they clung all the more to their idolatry and boasted in it.

entries.section: 3. Habakkuk has compassion on his people

paragraphs.text: 12 Art thou not from everlasting, O LORD my God, mine Holy One? We shall not die. O LORD, thou hast ordained them for judgment; and, O Rock, thou hast established them for correction. 13 Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon the plunderers, and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he? 14 And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them? 15 They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag: therefore they rejoice and are glad. 16 Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous. 17 Shall they therefore empty their net, and not spare continually to slay the nations?

The prophet Habakkuk, filled with zeal for the glory of God, so that he cried out and groaned, asking why God keeps silent about the wicked surrounding the righteous, corrupting his mind and his life, sees by the spirit of prophecy the fall of the Jewish people, marked at that time by injustice, falling under the bitter slavery of the Chaldeans, and he could not bear it. And as much as the prophet was marked by the openness of his heart toward God, speaking to Him frankly and boldly without formality or pretense, he was also marked by love for his people, so that he could not bear to see them suffering at the hands of a wicked and cruel nation, even if this was by divine permission for chastisement. He cannot bear the groans of his brethren and their bitterness, as though he says with the prophet Jeremiah: "For the hurt of the daughter of my people am I hurt; I mourn; astonishment hath taken hold on me" (Jer 8:21).

Truly, it is God who allows the chastisement of His children for their sins, but while He chastises, He does not accept that anyone should gloat over them, but requires us to groan with their groans and cry for their pains and be broken with their brokenness. God chastised Judah by the Babylonian captivity, and when the sons of Edom stood gloating, He rebuked them, saying: "But thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day of his calamity; neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress" (Obad 12).

As Habakkuk has compassion on his people fallen under the yoke of the Chaldeans, he reproaches God, saying: "Art thou not from everlasting, O LORD my God, mine Holy One?!" [12]. As though he says: How do You bear, O Lord, to see the Chaldeans, the wicked nation, plunder Your people and wrong them while You keep silent, though You are the Holy One who cannot bear evil?! You are my God, committed to my peace and security, not only for myself but for the whole people also. If You are my God who cares for me, will You not care for Your people?!

How beautiful are the prophet's feelings: in moments of bitter reproach he calls the Lord "my God, my Holy One," as though in his soul's distress he finds the Lord clinging to him, caring for him and embracing him as belonging to Him, for He is his own God and his own Holy One!

Let us reproach the Lord with all bitterness, but in our reproach let us see His clinging to us and His claiming us as His own, so that we cling all the more to Him and throw ourselves into His embrace, believing in His work with us and in us.

When our heart opens in love toward others and we intercede for them or ask on their behalf, the Lord becomes ours, for He clings to those who love and glories in His children whose hearts are enlarged!
The prophet continues his reproach, saying: "We shall not die. O LORD, thou hast ordained them for judgment; and, O Rock, thou hast established them for correction" [12].

The prophet says: "We shall not die," for he realized that the Lord, his God and his everlasting Holy One, in His love for His people pours His traits upon them, for since He is everlasting, above the limits of time, He gives His children "immortality"; they shall not die... Though in their evil they deserve death, in the living Lord they live. The Lord God says: "Because I live, ye shall live also" (Jn 14:19). He delivered them to the Chaldeans for chastisement, but as the psalmist says: "The LORD hath chastened me sore: but he hath not given me over unto death" (Ps 118:18).

God gave the Chaldeans the authority to chastise the people, and "to take the spoil, and to take the prey" (Isa 10:6), but not unlimited authority, but to the extent that God sees the salvation of His people in it, so the prophet says: "O LORD, thou hast ordained them for judgment; and, O Rock, thou hast established them for correction." So the limit of authority is that their work and plunder be for chastisement and judgment and not for destruction. Therefore when Satan asked the Lord to allow him to trouble Job, the Lord answered him: "Behold, he is in thine hand; but save his life" (Job 2:7). The Lord says to the sea: "Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed" (Job 38:11); He allows it to flow, but only to the limits that He set for it.

As for us, if God allows Satan to attack us, but within limits, we conquer by his attack if we are vigilant and thankful, so that the war becomes victory and triumph; and if we are slack and neglectful, Satan is not the cause of our harm; we are the cause. As St. John Chrysostom says: [Someone may say: Did not Adam get hurt, as his being was corrupted and he lost Paradise? No; the cause of this was the negligence of the one harmed, and his lack of self-control and striving. For Satan, who used various strong schemes, was unable to subdue Job; how then could he by a lesser means master Adam?!]

entries.section: 3. Habakkuk has compassion on his people

paragraphs.text: At the very time when the prophet declares his assurance that God, his holy and everlasting God, will not allow the people to die, but uses the Chaldeans for chastisement, he returns to reproach: "Thou art of purer eyes than to behold evil, and canst not look on iniquity: wherefore lookest thou upon the plunderers, and holdest thy peace when the wicked devoureth the man that is more righteous than he?!" [13].

The prophet Habakkuk knows what David the psalmist said: "For thou art not a God that hath pleasure in wickedness: neither shall evil dwell with thee" (Ps 5:4), and he understands what Jeremiah understood, that God hates the abominable thing (Jer 44:4), but he was perplexed how He could keep silent before what the wicked Chaldeans were doing to His people and look on the injustice, for the wicked had swallowed up one more righteous than himself. Here he does not say he swallowed up "the righteous," because the people were wicked, but compared with the Chaldeans they are more righteous than they.

Perhaps the word "look" or "behold" here does not mean mere seeing, for God knows all things, and nothing is hidden from Him; He has no need to look in order to see; rather, he means by it that He is pleased with their conduct and prospers their ways. For God's looking upon us means His caring for us and prospering our way.
The prophet began to bring out the traits of these wicked Chaldeans, whose way the Lord prospered for a time:
"And makest men as the fishes of the sea, as the creeping things, that have no ruler over them. They take up all of them with the angle, they catch them in their net, and gather them in their drag.
Therefore they rejoice and are glad.
Therefore they sacrifice unto their net, and burn incense unto their drag; because by them their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous (of the choicest - the Septuagint translation)

entries.section: 3. Habakkuk has compassion on his people

paragraphs.text: Shall they therefore empty their net, and not spare continually to slay the nations?" [14-17].

They looked at the other peoples as fish in the sea without an owner, with the right to catch what they please to eat and be satisfied, and as creeping things without authority, without price, to do with them what they wish. They rejoice and are glad when the hook brings up a fish or their nets gather many and men fall into their trap... They rejoice in human catches, offering idolatrous sacrifices and incense to their gods who grant them this precious catch. As though the prophet says to the Lord: Do You accept that Your people be fish without price in idolatrous nets, devoured by the wicked who offer sacrifices of thanks to the idols and incense before the idols?! Your people, in spite of what they have reached of deviation, are precious in Your eyes, so how can You leave them as prey for these Chaldeans?!

The nation of the Chaldeans rejoices in catching this people more than in catching any other people, for the prophet says: "because by them (by the angle and the net) their portion is fat, and their meat plenteous," or as it reads in the Septuagint, "their food is of the choicest," for it rejoices only in the choice catch. So the devil aims his arrows more at the best believers to draw them away from their faith, and as St. Jerome says: [Satan does not care for unbelievers, for they are outside... he wants only to corrupt the Church of Christ]

The wonder is that the enemy, the devil, like the Chaldeans, the fatter his portion becomes the more his greed increases and his heart is inflamed all the more to hunt others, for it is said: "Shall they therefore empty their net, and not spare continually to slay the nations?"

entries.section: 1. The prophet awaits the Lord's answer:

paragraphs.text: "I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer concerning my complaint!" [1].

Many questions often turn in our thoughts, and it befits us not only to present them to the Lord but also to stand as on a watchtower awaiting the Lord's answer to us. We stand as on a fortress, reassured by faith and sure confidence that God, the Lover of mankind, does not hide His mysteries from us and does only what is for our edification. Thus the prophet, after presenting his question, stood on the watchtower awaiting the voice of the Lord within him, and on the fortress took refuge in it, so that the question would not turn into a shaking of faith. This watchtower and this fortress are none other than the person of our Lord Jesus: through Him we understand the sublime divine mysteries as though from a sublime watchtower, and in Him we find refuge, for He is the true Rock upon which the Church was founded and in which she takes shelter. He is the watchtower without whom we do not know the Father, as He says: "Neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son, and he to whom the Son will reveal him" (Mt 11:27). And He is the Rock in which the Church takes refuge like a gentle dove, to whom He calls: "O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock, in the secret places of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice" (Song 2:14).

St. Jerome sees that when Habakkuk stands as on a watchtower to watch and take his stand, and takes refuge as in a tower, he does so as a spiritual soldier who struggles against the devil without surrender. He contemplates the works of God and His mysteries, especially the Cross, and is filled with strength for the spiritual war against evil.

entries.section: 2. The Lord's concern for the question:

paragraphs.text: 2 And the LORD answered me, and said, "Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it. 3 For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.

As long as the soul seeks and stands to watch for the words of the Lord and His answers, taking refuge in Him as in a fortress, taking its stand for spiritual striving through divine knowledge, He in turn does not withhold from it. The prophet says: "And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it. For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry" [2-3].

It is as though the Lord requires of him not to come to Him with a pen and paper to write what he sees and hears, but that there is need of tables on which the word of God is engraved in a clear script that draws the one who looks at it, so that he comes running to it... Moreover, the clarity of the script enables even those who are running to read it. In Isaiah it is said: "Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever" (Isa 30:8). Moreover, the vision may not be fulfilled immediately but at the appointed time, in the fullness of time; therefore it befits the prophet to wait, confident that it will surely come, even if it seems to be delayed.

What is this vision of which he speaks here, if not the one concerning the mystery of the Cross, which is fulfilled in the fullness of time when the Word of God becomes incarnate? He recorded divine love, not with ink and paper, but with His shed blood, and drew it on the two tables of the Cross, or its two beams, the vertical and the horizontal, drawing all to Himself.

Let us run in the Holy Spirit to the Cross to read what the Only-Begotten Son has engraved, declaring to us the sublime divine mysteries! Here we do not find the wicked Chaldeans perishing; rather, the devil himself and all his demons have utterly collapsed, and every authority they had usurped has been shattered.

entries.section: 3. The punishment of the Chaldeans:

paragraphs.text: When the Lord lifts up His prophet Habakkuk to the vision of the Cross, which shatters the kingdom of the devil, He goes on to reveal the works of the devil in the life of the wicked Chaldeans, which the Cross shatters. It is as though He reveals to us the evil planting which the Father did not plant but which is the sowing of the enemy of good, of which the Lord said that it must be uprooted (Mt 15:13). These evil plantings which He shatters are:

entries.section: First: Pride and inner emptiness:

paragraphs.text: 4 "Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith. 5 Yea also, wine is treacherous; the man is proud, and does not rest. He who has enlarged his desire as hell, and is as death, and cannot be satisfied, but gathers unto him all nations, and heaps unto him all people: 6 Shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say, Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long? and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay! 7 Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and awake that shall vex thee, and thou shalt be for booties unto them? 8 Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee; because of men's blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein.
"Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith. Yea also, wine is treacherous. The proud man does not rest" [4-5].

Although God permitted His people to be disciplined by means of the pagan Chaldeans, the Chaldeans became arrogant and thought that they had conquered and triumphed by their own power and might. Therefore God accomplishes His purpose through them, namely the discipline of His children, and then returns to punish them for the pride of their heart. As it was said by Isaiah the prophet concerning Assyria, that it is the rod of God's anger and the staff in their hand is His indignation (Isa 10:5), He accomplishes His purpose through them... "Wherefore it shall come to pass, that when the Lord hath performed his whole work upon mount Zion and on Jerusalem, I will punish the fruit of the stout heart of the king of Assyria, and the glory of his high looks. For he saith, By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom; for I am prudent: and I have removed the bounds of the people, and have robbed their treasures, and I have put down the inhabitants like a valiant man: and my hand hath found as a nest the riches of the people: and as one gathereth eggs that are left, have I gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved the wing, or opened the mouth, or peeped. Shall the axe boast itself against him that heweth therewith? or shall the saw magnify itself against him that shaketh it? as if the rod should shake itself against them that lift it up, or as if the staff should lift up itself, as if it were no wood" (Isa 10:12-15).

This is the work of the devil in the life of man... pride, so that man thinks that by his own power and wisdom he accomplishes his purpose, and does not realize that every energy and possibility is from God, even if man distorts its nature and turns it away from its purpose.

By pride the devil fell from his angelic rank and descended to the depths of the abyss (Isa 14:12; Obad 4); therefore he does not cease to strike humanity with the same disease, to bring it down with him from the life of faith, to make it lose the enjoyment of the divine Kingdom, and to cast it down to a level beneath the animal. St. John Chrysostom says: [He who exalts himself in his thought, lofty above men, is found lower than the irrational creation].
If the wicked man perishes through satanic pride, "the just shall live by his faith."

Scholars see that this phrase, "the just shall live by his faith," is the heart and sinew of Habakkuk's prophecy, and as it has been said, "these famous words sum up the whole vision." The Apostle Paul quoted it to affirm that justification is not possible by the works of the Law but by faith in Christ Jesus, as we are hidden in His righteousness. St. Augustine says: [In Him we rise, and in Him we go forth to the Father, to become perfect in an invisible way and justified]. Righteousness is not a collection; it requires sound faith that is not deviant, and as St. Augustine says: [Where there is no sound faith there is no righteousness, for the just shall live by faith].

Let us return to the pride which the enemy of good sows in us to deprive us of the true life of faith and to remove us from the righteousness that is in Christ Jesus. We find that this empty pride gives the soul a kind of inner hunger or thirst, through which man seeks to be satisfied not from the righteousness of God but from everything earthly, through injustice and plunder... and the more he receives, the more his inner emptiness increases, so that he remains unsatisfied all the days of his life.

In this spirit the Chaldeans attacked the nations, hunted humanity and humiliated them, without true satisfaction: "He who enlarged his desire as hell, and is as death, and cannot be satisfied, but gathers unto him all nations, and heaps unto him all evils; shall not all these take up a parable against him, and a taunting proverb against him, and say to him that increaseth that which is not his, How long?! and to him that ladeth himself with thick clay: Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and awake that shall vex thee, and thou shalt be for booties unto them?! Because thou hast spoiled many nations, all the remnant of the people shall spoil thee; because of men's blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein" [5-9].

If we take the literal interpretation, we say that the Chaldeans enlarged their souls like the grave, swallowing peoples like the dead and never being satisfied. They were in continual motion to plunder nations and peoples by injustice without ceasing. But this work has an end; the balances are overturned and the captive nations are set free, to stand in mockery of the Chaldeans and to deride them, saying:

"Woe to him that increaseth that which is not his! how long?"... They pour woes upon the Chaldeans, who thought they had gained much, but in truth it is not theirs; they are returning what they had counted as spoil!

"That ladeth himself with thick clay" (pledges)... What they gathered is not wealth but thick clay; it is not gold and silver, but they gathered dust that weighs down their souls with the love of the earthly world.

"Shall they not rise up suddenly that shall bite thee, and awake that shall vex thee?" In a moment the Chaldeans do not expect, while they are utterly secure, those who were as though asleep rise up, so that the Chaldeans become booty for them, after the Chaldeans had earlier taken them as booty. As they spoiled the nations, the nations spoil them; as they shed blood, their blood is shed; and as they wrought havoc on the land and the cities, havoc is wrought on them.

The matter does not stop at the satiety of the Chaldeans; rather, they lose what they thought was a gain for them, and they lose their wealth and their dignity... It is said to them: "As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head" (Obad 15).

If man thinks that sin, with its lusts and pleasures, satisfies the soul, in truth it brings him into a state of inner emptiness, hunger and thirst... So man runs to it to drink from it as from the salt waters of the sea, which increase his thirst and even make him lose his very life.

entries.section: Second: Evil gain:

paragraphs.text: "9 Woe to him that coveteth an evil covetousness to his house, that he may set his nest on high, that he may be delivered from the power of evil! 10 Thou hast consulted shame to thy house by cutting off many people, and hast sinned against thy soul. 11 For the stone shall cry out of the wall, and the beam out of the timber shall answer it" [9-11].

This is the second woe. The first was because of the sin of pride, which does not satisfy the soul but destroys it; the second is because of the love of evil gain. The wicked man thinks that he fills his house with good things, and does not realize that he is gathering evil gain that brings a curse upon his whole house. The wise man says: "He that is greedy of gain (the covetous) troubleth his own house" (Prov 15:8). He gathers evil gain, reckoning that it will fly him to where no one can approach him, so that he builds his nest on high, but he finds that he is building his house with shame, and so he sins against his own soul. The stones he acquired with the money of injustice to build the house cry out, witnessing to his evil, and the wooden beams by which the building holds together do not keep silent. The house that he builds with the money of injustice turns into a sorrowful instrument that sings a lament over its owner.

King Ahab and his wife Jezebel thought that they had killed Naboth the Jezreelite and inherited his vineyard, with no one to question them and no one to watch their conduct, but they only acquired their own destruction, for the word of the Lord to Ahab through Elijah the prophet was: "In the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth shall dogs lick thy blood, even thine" (1 Kgs 21:19).

entries.section: Third: Violence:

paragraphs.text: "12 Woe to him that buildeth a town with blood, and stablisheth a city by iniquity! 13 Behold, is it not of the LORD of hosts that the people shall labour in the very fire, and the people shall weary themselves for very vanity? 14 For the earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD, as the waters cover the sea" [12-14].

This is the third woe, which falls upon the man who, in his love of evil gain or ugly profit, turns into a ravening beast, so that he builds his city by shedding blood and establishes his town by the law of iniquity. St. John Chrysostom says: [Man has become worse than the wild beasts, for they do not eat one another so long as they are of the same kind; but man devours his brother in humanity, and thinks that he cannot build a city in which to rest except at the expense of his brother's blood!]

In any case, the earth is filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord when the world sees that the unjust shedders of blood have labored not to raise cities or establish towns but to become fuel for the fire, laboring in vain until sickness strikes them from exhaustion, and to no profit!

If our bodies, through shedding blood or through their iniquity, have become earth, then, when they receive the sanctification of the Spirit, they are filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord and bear the meek Spirit of their Savior; and if our life has become a salt sea, the sweet waters of the Holy Spirit transform its nature.

Finally, if injustice reaches its utmost ugliness when man becomes a shedder of blood, St. Jerome sees that the heretics are the worst shedders of blood: they do not kill the body but the souls, by deviation from the living faith, that is, from the truth, for he says: [The lying heretic kills many souls by deceiving them... He is a deceiver and thirsty for blood].

entries.section: Fourth: Drunkenness:

paragraphs.text: 15 "Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that pourest out thy wrath and makest him drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness! 16 Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the LORD's right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory. 17 For the violence of Lebanon shall cover thee, and the spoil of beasts, which made them afraid, because of men's blood, and for the violence of the land, of the city, and of all that dwell therein.

"Woe unto him that giveth his neighbour drink, that pourest out thy wrath and makest him drunken also, that thou mayest look on their nakedness! Thou art filled with shame for glory: drink thou also, and let thy foreskin be uncovered: the cup of the LORD's right hand shall be turned unto thee, and shameful spewing shall be on thy glory" [15-16].

The fourth woe is for the sin of drunkenness. The one who becomes drunk, finding that he has lost his true dignity and inner balance, offers it to his companion, pouring out the bottle for him in order to tempt him by its sight, so that, as he himself has lost his purity, he wants to look on the nakedness of his brother, that is, his inner secrets, in order to corrupt him in his depths.

Who is the one who offers drunkenness if not the enemy of good, who draws man with his enticements as though he were his companion, in order to make him lose his true Christ and put him in a state of shame? This conduct does not add glory to the enemy but shame; if he thinks that by it he establishes his kingdom and widens its bounds, he only fills the cup of God's wrath against himself, to drink of the bitterness that he offered us, doubled: "in the cup which she hath filled fill to her double" (Rev 18:3, 6).

entries.section: Fourth: Drunkenness:

paragraphs.text: "Shameful spewing shall be on thy glory" [16]. Thus those around him look at him and find in him no true glory and no sincere wealth, so they vomit upon his vain glory! Thus the one who gives others of the intoxication of sin is only preparing for himself one who will vomit on him and shame him!

What we say about the intoxication of sin, to which the devil draws us, we say also about the life of luxury and indulgence, the life that carries within it the death of the soul and shame instead of outward glory. As St. John Chrysostom says: [The man who lives in pleasures is dead while he is alive, for he lives only for his belly... Is not he who spends his time in banquets and drunkenness dead, and buried in darkness?!].

entries.section: Fifth: Idolatry:

paragraphs.text: "18 What profiteth the graven image that the maker thereof hath graven it; the molten image, and a teacher of lies, that the maker of his work trusteth therein, to make dumb idols? 19 Woe unto him that saith to the wood, Awake; to the dumb stone, Arise!
Shall it teach? Behold, it is laid over with gold and silver, and there is no breath at all in the midst of it. 20 But the LORD is in his holy temple:
let all the earth keep silence before him" [18-20].

This is the last woe, which was directed against the Chaldeans, who boasted in their gods, which are the work of their hands. Truly they reveal cleverness in craftsmanship and skill in work, and they spent much to set them up, for they are overlaid with gold and silver, but inside they are stones, without spirit or life!

What will these idols profit them on the day of their punishment?! They asked the enemy, that is, the wooden Baal, to awake and save them, and the stone goddess Ashtoreth, the wife of the god Baal, to take heed of what had befallen them and to take pity on their condition, but neither is able to save. They are two gods fair to look upon but utterly powerless, whereas the true God is in His holy temple, and the earth cannot stand before Him.

Strange is the man who leaves his God, who dwells in his heart as in a heavenly temple, and pursues his own thoughts as though they were pagan gods, beautiful in appearance and shining, but lifeless and unable to offer salvation.

entries.section: Fifth: Idolatry:

paragraphs.text: Wretched is the man who rejects the Giver of salvation, who makes of his heart a heaven, and worships deceitful human thoughts and philosophies, which make of him earth... He cannot resist the Lord when he hears the voice: "Let all the earth keep silence before him" [20].
May we not be earth that is silent and dumb before God, but a spiritual heaven that bears the word of God, joyful heavenly voices, and an angelic hymn that never ceases.

entries.section: 1. The works of God through the years:

paragraphs.text: "1 A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet upon Shigionoth (strings): 2 O LORD, I have heard thy speech, and was afraid.
O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy" [1-2].

When the prophet stood on the watchtower awaiting the word of God, and took his stand on the divine tower, taking refuge, his soul rejoiced within him in spite of all the harsh circumstances surrounding him. And while the prophet was groaning for the sake of the people of God, God revealed to him His plan of salvation through the ages, which was manifested on the Cross, so he rejoiced, taking hold of the harp of the Spirit to strike its strings with a psalm of praise, saying:

"O LORD, I have heard thy speech (thy word), and was afraid." It is as though he says: O Lord, when I heard Your word my soul was filled with awe and fear; You revealed Your mysteries to me and I understood Your works, and I was amazed!

His vision did not stop at the limits of God's works in his own age, but extended to see them through the ages, realizing that God in His love, though He is angry and disciplines, yet even in His anger cannot bear the groaning of His people, but returns and has mercy. "O LORD, revive thy work in the midst of the years, in the midst of the years make known; in wrath remember mercy." Truly the Lord is angry at the evil of man, but in the midst of His anger His mercies groan, a matter that the prophet Hosea expressed in a wonderful image, saying on the tongue of the Lord: "Mine heart is turned within me, my repentings are kindled together. I will not execute the fierceness of mine anger, I will not return to destroy Ephraim: for I am God, and not man; the Holy One in the midst of thee: and I will not come in wrath" (Hos 11:8-9).

Although God is a hidden God, or one who hides Himself, as Isaiah the prophet said (Isa 45:15), He reveals Himself to His people through the generations by His mercies, which He shows even in moments of divine anger and discipline... Perhaps what God presents through the years in the way of revelations is shown in practice in the change of humanity that had been corrupted and which He raised from its fall. As St. Jerome says: [God works wonders every day; He is at work... You are the wonderful works of God; yesterday you were seizing what belonged to others, and today you give to others what is yours". This change is the goal of the word of God revealed through the Mosaic Law, which was manifested in its fullness through the incarnation of the divine Word and His declaration of salvation on the Cross. For this reason the prophet returns to the works of God with His people in the wilderness, with the giving of the Law on Mount Moses, in order to proceed with them to His works through the Messiah the Savior.

entries.section: 2. The works of God on Mount Sinai:

paragraphs.text: 3 God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran. Selah. His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise. 4 And his brightness was as the light; he had horns coming out of his hand: and there was the hiding of his power. 5 Before him went the pestilence, and burning coals went forth at his feet. 6 He stood, and measured the earth: he beheld, and drove asunder the nations; and the everlasting mountains were scattered, the perpetual hills did bow: his ways are everlasting. 7 I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction: and the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble. 8 Was the LORD displeased against the rivers? was thine anger against the rivers? was thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses and thy chariots of salvation? 9 Thy bow was made quite naked, the sevenfold arrows are thy word. Selah. Thou didst cleave the earth with rivers. 10 The mountains saw thee, and they trembled: the overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high. 11 The sun and moon stood still in their habitation: at the light of thine arrows they went, and at the shining of thy glittering spear. 12 Thou didst march through the land in indignation, thou didst thresh the heathen in anger.

The heart of the prophet Habakkuk was drawn to the work of God when Moses went up on the mountain to receive the Law, and the mountain was filled with splendor and glory, and God shone with His light upon His people, so that his heart and tongue, his soul and body, were set free in joy and praise, saying:
"God came from Teman, and the Holy One from mount Paran. Selah.
His glory covered the heavens, and the earth was full of his praise" [3].

He points here to the appearance of God in His glory in a tangible way when Moses received the Law, as it is said: "The LORD came down upon mount Sinai" (Ex 19:20), "And the sight of the glory of the LORD was like devouring fire on the top of the mount" (Ex 24:17), "The LORD came from Sinai, and rose up from Seir unto them; he shined forth from mount Paran" (Deut 33:2).

When He came to us through the Law, His splendor covered the heavens, and the earth was filled with His praise. What are these heavens and earth if not the human soul and body, which are sanctified by the word of God, so that the soul shines with the glory of the Lord and the body is filled with joy and exultation? Through the divine Word the soul is filled with divine light and heavenly knowledge, while the body, with all its members, is turned into a harp in the hands of the Holy Spirit, on which He plays a unique, heavenly hymn. In other words, God is manifested in the whole of man's life, in his soul as in his body. St. Jerome says: [Sing true praise; sing psalms with every part of your being. Let your hand sing by giving, and your foot by hastening to do good... Let all your strings give a sound, for if one string stops the harp loses its being. What does it profit you if you are chaste but covetous?! What do you gain if you are pure and generous in giving but at the same time envious?! What is your benefit if six of your strings are sound and the seventh is broken?! For one broken string deprives the harp of its ability to give a complete sound].

In the Septuagint it reads: "God cometh from the south, and the Holy One from the shady mountain," and St. Jerome comments on this phrase: "God comes from the south. Here he points to the Savior, for God was born in the south, because Bethlehem is south of Jerusalem." St. Didymus the Blind sees that the south points to the hot winds that blow upon the soul and inflame it with the Spirit, or with love, so that it is not cold, while the north points to the cold northern winds, which point to the work of Satan, who spoils the warmth of the Spirit; therefore in the Song of Songs the bride asked that the north wind, which is the work of the devil, be removed from her, and that the south wind come to her, which points to the Savior, her Bridegroom Himself.

entries.section: 2. The works of God on Mount Sinai:

paragraphs.text: The prophet continues his hymn, saying: "And his brightness was as the light; he had horns coming out of his hand: and there was the hiding of his power" [4]. It is as though he says: I used to think that matters went on without direction, the wicked devouring the righteous, and the nation of the Chaldeans swallowing the rest of the peoples, with no one to call it to account and no one to restrain it; but when I understood the mysteries of Your knowledge, I found You to be the eternal Light who comprehends hidden mysteries, with nothing hidden from Your eyes. You stretch out Your hand to work, and a ray comes forth from it that exposes those who walk in darkness; then all understand Your power, which was hidden for a time.

The phrase "he had horns coming out of his hand" means the light of the rays of the sun, as it appears in the translation of the Jesuits. These two horns in His hand are the two tables of the Law, which the prophet Moses received, as it is said: "from his right hand went a fiery law for them" (Deut 23:2).

entries.section: 2. The works of God on Mount Sinai:

paragraphs.text: "Before him went the pestilence, and burning coals (fever) went forth at his feet" [5].
By His appearing He drives out the pestilence of evil and darkness, and at His feet, that is, with authority, He commands the fever and it obeys Him.

entries.section: 2. The works of God on Mount Sinai:

paragraphs.text: "He stood, and measured the earth: he beheld, and drove asunder the nations; and the everlasting mountains were scattered, the perpetual hills did bow: his ways are everlasting" [6].

He stands to measure the earth, for it is His creation for which He cares; for its sake He stands to work and does not rest until He declares His judgments, so that the wicked nations tremble and the lofty mountains and the ancient hills are crushed. He is the Everlasting One who orders all things to work in the good time. It is as though he says: I used to think the world was like a sea full of fish that the wicked nation hunts without restraint, but I have realized that nothing is hidden from You.

If the earth, as we said before, points to the body, then God stood to measure it as a sign of His care for it and His sanctifying it, so that the pagan nations dwelling there tremble, that is, every evil and spiritual weakness is removed from the body, and the lofty mountains are crushed, that is, the sins that seem extremely violent, which no one can move. Before God the hills of the body that weigh down the soul are shaken.

Here the prophet describes God as standing: "He stood, and measured the earth." As St. Jerome says: [God does not change and has no bodily postures, but He is said to stand when He deals with the righteous, and He is said to appear walking when Adam fell (Gen 3:9), and sitting as Judge and King (Isa 6:1), and sleeping, as in the boat, when man is amid the storms of temptation, and He appears standing, as it is said, "God standeth in the congregation of the mighty." He is therefore speaking here of the earth, which has enjoyed the gladness of His salvation and has been sanctified by it, so He appeared standing to measure it!

entries.section: 2. The works of God on Mount Sinai:

paragraphs.text: I saw the tents of Cushan in affliction: and the curtains of the land of Midian did tremble" [7].

The name "tents of Cushan" is not mentioned in the Old Testament except in this phrase; it may be an ancient name for Midian that was abandoned. Thus, if the vision of God is manifested to Habakkuk, and the Lord in his eyes is coming from Mount Sinai, then everything that resists Him collapses before Him.
Perhaps the tents of Cushan appeared as though under affliction and the curtains of Midian trembling when God gave the land of Canaan to His people, and all the surrounding nations trembled.

Some think that the tents of Cushan came under affliction when the Lord delivered Cushan into the hand of the judge Othniel the son of Kenaz after Israel had served him eight years (Judg 3:8-11), and the power of God was manifested in His judge sent for the salvation of His people, and He humbled the one who had enslaved His people. As for the trembling of the curtains of Midian, it happened when the companion of Gideon saw a dream: "a cake of barley bread tumbled into the host of Midian, and came unto a tent, and smote it that it fell, and overturned it, that the tent lay along" (Judg 7:3), and that was a sign of the sword of Gideon the son of Joash, who slew the Midianites.
In short, Habakkuk praises the Lord for His works, in that He gives His children victory and triumph, and even authority, so that the demons tremble before them and come under affliction!

entries.section: 2. The works of God on Mount Sinai:

paragraphs.text: "Was the LORD displeased against the rivers?! was thine anger against the rivers, or thy wrath against the sea, that thou didst ride upon thine horses and thy chariots of salvation?!" [8].

If many waters point to peoples (Rev 17:15), then the people of God are likened to rivers, where the water is sweet, and the pagan nations to the salt seas. When God disciplines His people, His anger is kindled against the rivers because of the injustice found in their midst, and when He punishes the nations in His wrath because of the evils they committed against His people, His anger is kindled against the seas.

His anger was kindled against the rivers and seas when they stood in the way of His people in their crossing from the land of Egypt to the Promised Land, so He divided the Red Sea and the River Jordan, passing through with His people as with chariots of salvation, as though He were the leader of the procession of salvation that brings them across from the slavery of the devil to His heavenly Kingdom, while the believers are the horses who carry God, their Leader, within them. St. Jerome says in this regard: [This is said of God, if we are the horses of God on which He rides]. And Father Theophan the Recluse says: [He fights for you Himself, and delivers your enemies into your hands whenever He wills, however He wills, as it is written: "For the LORD thy God walketh in the midst of thy camp, to deliver thee, and to give up thine enemies before thee" (Deut 23:4)].

entries.section: 2. The works of God on Mount Sinai:

paragraphs.text: "Thy bow was made quite naked, the sevenfold arrows are thy words. Selah" [9].

What is the bow that was made naked to strike like sevenfold arrows, if not the divine Incarnation, through which we enjoyed the Word of God as an arrow that shatters the evil that had reigned within us?! May the Word of God dwell in us as a true arrow that wounds our hearts with love, so that we say, "I am sick of love" (Song 2:5), and removes from them all the malignant corruption which the wicked enemy established in them.
The words of the Lord are "sevenfold"; they enter the heart and make it perfect, for the number 7 points to perfection.
"Thou didst cleave the earth with rivers" [9].

When we receive the incarnate Word in us as a divine arrow that wounds our hearts with love and removes their corruption, He in turn, seeing that they have become earth and not heaven, loving the temporal rather than the eternal, cleaves it through fellowship in the Cross and suffering, and turns the earth into rivers of living water, as the Savior said: "He that believeth on me, as the scripture hath said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water" (Jn 7:38).

Let us not fear that we are a barren land, for the Lord by His Cross causes the springs of His Holy Spirit to burst forth in us like rivers of living water, which water our land and overflow with witness to Him in every place!

St. Jerome sees that the Lord Christ is the original River who pours into our land rivers that are the fruit of His work in us; these rivers bear witness to the true River, praising Him not by words only but also by deeds, as the Psalmist says: "Let the floods clap their hands" (Ps 98:8). "May the rivers that are watered from the Source, Jesus, clap their hands, for the work of the saints is the praise of God. Christ is not praised by words but by deeds; He asks for action, not for voice."

entries.section: 2. The works of God on Mount Sinai:

paragraphs.text: "The mountains saw thee, and they trembled: the overflowing of the water passed by: the deep uttered his voice, and lifted up his hands on high" [10].

If the living Word of God cleaves our earth by His Cross and makes it rivers of water that praise Him and sing to Him by true spiritual work, then, in His dwelling within us, the mountains of our heavy sins see Him and flee in fear from before His face. What we used to count as firm mountains that no one could move become, by the Cross, a plain. As it is said in Zechariah: "Who art thou, O great mountain? before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain: and he shall bring forth the headstone thereof with shoutings among the shouters, honor, honor to it" (Zech 4:7). We have seen in our study of the book of Zechariah how the evil mountain disappears so that the Lord Christ appears as the cornerstone, the honored One, cut out without hands, since He is not of the seed of man, and becomes a mountain that fills the whole earth (Dan 2:35). By this the grace of God flows like boundless waters to give a voice of inner praise, and the two inner hands of the soul are lifted on high to practice the heavenly work.

"The sun and moon stood still in their habitation: at the light of thine arrows they went, and at the shining of thy glittering spear. Thou didst march through the land in indignation, thou didst thresh the heathen in anger.
Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed" [11-13].

As the prophet praises God for His works through the years, he recalls the days of Joshua, when he prayed that the sun and moon should stand still in their places in heaven until Israel's victory over its enemies was completed (Josh 10:12-13), so that no swift night should come in which the enemy would flee before the defeat was accomplished. In the light Joshua defeated the enemy, and so, when the Lord shines in the heart as the Sun of Righteousness, and the battlefield is turned into a moon, being the holy Church that resists the devil, the light scatters the darkness of the enemy, and the Lord remains shining until the victory is completely achieved.

Perhaps he also means that all nature is subject to God's work of salvation, so that even the sun and moon work together according to His plan to establish His kingdom of light and destroy the kingdom of darkness.

We can say that "the sun and moon stood still in their habitation" on the day of the Cross, when they vanished before the splendor of the glory of the Sun of Righteousness, in shame at what humanity was doing to Him. They stood hidden, astonished also at how the Lord Christ shatters the devil and all his hosts to free man from them as from pagan nations, saying: "In anger thou didst thresh the heathen; thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, for salvation with thine anointed."

entries.section: 3. The joy of salvation:

paragraphs.text: 13 Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed; thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck. Selah. 14 Thou didst strike through with his staves the head of his villages: they came out as a whirlwind to scatter me: their rejoicing was as to devour the poor secretly. 15 Thou didst walk through the sea with thine horses, through the heap of great waters. 16 When I heard, my belly trembled; my lips quivered at the voice: rottenness entered into my bones, and I trembled in myself, that I might rest in the day of trouble: when he cometh up unto the people, he will invade them with his troops. 17 Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; the labour of the olive shall fail, and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls: 18 Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. 19 The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places.
"Thou wentest forth for the salvation of thy people, even for salvation with thine anointed.
Thou woundedst the head out of the house of the wicked, by discovering the foundation unto the neck. Selah.
Thou didst strike through with his staves the head of his villages" [13-14].

The prophet concludes his hymn by revealing God's salvation for man, by shattering the devil's authority over us and by raising up the spirit of joy in us. By the Cross He crushed the head of the house of the wicked devil, which was laid bare down to the foundation, and his hidden deceits appeared, exposing him from the foundation to the neck. If the enemy aimed his arrows against us, it was only so that they would turn back upon him and shatter him completely, so that he would have no authority over us and no place in us.
The Fathers have often spoken to us about the shattering of the devil's authority in order to raise in us hope for spiritual work without fear or wavering. Among their words:

* On the Cross Christ put Satan and all his army to shame. Be sure that Christ was crucified in His body on the Cross, and by it He crucified Satan there... The Cross was a sign of victory and a banner of triumph. His purpose in being lifted up on the Cross was to lift us up from the earth, and as I think, the Cross of the Savior is the ladder that Jacob saw.

St. Jerome * We learn the art of war so that we can struggle not against men but against spirits. Indeed, if we had a (true) mind we would never struggle; we struggle because we have chosen this, although we have received authority from the One who dwells in us, who said, "Behold, I give unto you power to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy" (Lk 10:19). He has given you all authority to struggle or not to struggle, if you wish. We struggle because we are slack, but the Apostle Paul did not struggle; rather he says: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?" (Rom 8:35). Listen also to his words: "And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly" (Rom 16:20). He bore authority when he said: "I command thee in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her" (Acts 16:18). This is not the language of one who struggles, for he who struggles has not yet conquered, and he who conquers no longer struggles.

* If we wish, God makes him trodden under our feet, but what contempt and misery it is to see him tread on the heads of those to whom it was given to trample him under their feet?! How does this happen?! It is because of us. If we wish, he is great, and if we wish, he is of little cunning. If we are watchful and stand beside our King, he withdraws, and in his war against us he is no more than a little child.

St. John Chrysostom This is the secret of the joy of the prophet's soul, when he saw God's saving work in shattering the devil's authority for the sake of the kingdom of light. Truly his inward parts trembled when he saw the Chaldeans spoiling all fruit, but behind this discipline there is a greater good, when God turns discipline into the joy of salvation.

entries.section: 3. The joy of salvation:

paragraphs.text: The prophet says: "When I heard, my belly trembled; my lips quivered at the voice: rottenness entered into my bones, and I trembled in myself, that I might rest in the day of trouble: when he cometh up unto the people, he will invade them with his troops" [16]. He saw the Chaldeans as a people who crowd upon them or as an enemy who wishes to destroy them, so his belly trembled, his lips quivered, and rottenness entered into his bones... The enemy has spoiled all spiritual fruit, so the fig tree does not blossom and the vines bear no fruit, and the olive trees have dried up. This is the picture of man fallen under the devil, who does not enjoy the unity of the Spirit (the fig tree), nor the work of the Cross (the vines that are pressed), nor inner peace (the olive); that is, he loses his inner life by being deprived of the work of the Holy Spirit and of attachment to the Cross of our Lord Jesus. And the matter does not stop at the corruption of the inner depths, but even the body loses its holiness and becomes like dead animals, for he says: "and the fields shall yield no meat; the flock shall be cut off from the fold, and there shall be no herd in the stalls" [17]. The body finds no spiritual food, so it hungers and falls ill and even dies spiritually, and man becomes like a fold without flock and a stall without herd! This is what the enemy desires, the loss of the holiness of the soul and also of the body.

But God does not leave man thus; rather, He restores his salvation to him, giving him the joy of salvation, offering Himself as his strength, and making his feet firm to run toward heaven swiftly like hinds, so that man walks upon the holy heights and does not descend into the mire of the world and its dust, for he says:

entries.section: 3. The joy of salvation:

paragraphs.text: "Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation. The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds' feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places. To the chief singer on my stringed instruments" [18-19].

Thus the book began with pain and distress with bitterness because of inner and outer troubles, but when the prophet entered into an open dialogue with God and stood as on a watchtower awaiting, and on a fortress taking his stand to see the works of God, the book ended with joy and gladness, as he realized that God Himself is the strength of His children, who strengthens their feet and lifts them to the heights to carry them by His Holy Spirit above all events.
